title: Y-Row, W-Row & N — や ゆ よ わ を ん

points.name: や
points.explanation: The syllable や produces a 'ya' sound like the 'ya' in 'yacht' or 'yard'. It's formed by starting with a 'y' glide (your tongue near the palate, as if beginning the 'ee' sound) and quickly moving into the open 'ah' vowel. The Y-row only has three members in Japanese (ya, yu, yo) — there are no yi or ye sounds in the standard syllabary. Beyond appearing in words, や is important because its smaller form ゃ is used in combination characters like しゃ (sha), きゃ (kya), and many others that you'll learn soon.
rules: Start with a 'y' glide (tongue near palate) and quickly open to 'ah'.
The Y-row has only three sounds: ya, yu, yo — no yi or ye in standard Japanese.
Small ゃ (combined with other kana) creates sounds like しゃ (sha), きゃ (kya), etc.

examples.english: hilly area / uptown (as in Yamanote Line)

points.name: ゆ
points.explanation: The syllable ゆ produces a 'yu' sound like the 'yu' in 'yule' or 'you' — but remember to keep the 'u' vowel flat and unrounded, without the strong lip-rounding of English 'you'. Start with the 'y' glide (tongue near palate) and transition into the Japanese 'u' vowel. ゆ appears in beautiful vocabulary: ゆき (snow), ゆめ (dream), ゆか (floor), and ゆかた (a light cotton kimono). Like や, its small form ゅ is used in combination characters: しゅ (shu), きゅ (kyu), and others.
rules: 'Y' glide into the Japanese 'u' vowel — keep lips flat, not rounded like English 'you'.
Small ゅ creates combination syllables like しゅ (shu), じゅ (ju), きゅ (kyu).
ゆき (snow) and ゆめ (dream) are poetic vocabulary words that appear early in learning.

points.name: よ
points.explanation: The syllable よ produces a 'yo' sound as in 'yoke' or the English greeting 'yo'. Form the 'y' glide and move into the 'oh' vowel, stopping cleanly. よ appears in extremely common vocabulary: よこ (side / horizontal), よそ (elsewhere / another place), よめ (bride / daughter-in-law), and よし (alright! — an exclamation of resolve or satisfaction). Like the other Y-row members, よ has a small form (ょ) used in combination syllables like しょ (sho), きょ (kyo), and ちょ (cho).
rules: 'Y' glide into a clean 'oh' vowel — stop cleanly without gliding to 'w'.
Small ょ creates combination syllables like しょ (sho), きょ (kyo), ちょ (cho).
よし! is a common exclamation of resolution or satisfaction — 'alright!' or 'here we go!'.

points.name: わ
points.explanation: The syllable わ produces a 'wa' sound as in 'water' or 'want'. The W-row in modern Japanese has only one active member — わ — since the other W-row sounds (wi, we, wo) have all merged with their vowel equivalents in modern Japanese. The 'w' glide in わ is gentle: start with slightly rounded lips (as if beginning 'oo'), then quickly open to the 'ah' vowel. わ is most commonly encountered as the start of わたし (I/me) — probably the first word most Japanese learners ever look up.
rules: Gentle 'w' glide into the 'ah' vowel — lips start slightly rounded, then open wide.
The W-row in modern Japanese has only one commonly used member: わ.
わたし (I / me) is the most important word using わ — you'll use it constantly.

points.name: を
points.explanation: The character を is almost always pronounced simply as 'o' in modern Japanese — the 'w' before it has disappeared from everyday speech, though some traditional or theatrical speakers still say 'wo'. を has exactly one job in Japanese: it's the direct object particle, marking the noun that receives the action of a verb. For example, ほんをよむ means 'to read a book' (literally 'book [object marker] to read'). You will never see を used as part of a regular word — it exists solely as this grammatical particle. Understanding を is essential for building even the simplest Japanese sentences.
rules: Pronounced 'o' in modern Japanese (not 'wo') — it sounds identical to the vowel お.
を is used exclusively as the direct object particle — it always comes after a noun receiving an action.
Example: ほんをよむ = 'to read a book'; みせをみる = 'to look at the store'.

examples.english: to read a book (を marks ほん as the object)
to look at the store (を marks みせ)
to buy an umbrella (を marks かさ)
to listen to a sound (を marks おと)

points.flashcardAnswer: o (or wo) — the direct object particle; pronounced 'o' in modern Japanese

points.name: ん
points.shortDescription: A syllabic 'n' — one full beat of sound
points.explanation: The character ん is unique in the hiragana syllabary: it's the only character that represents a consonant by itself, without a vowel. ん is a syllabic nasal — it takes up a full beat in the rhythm of Japanese speech. Its exact sound varies depending on what comes after it: before 'b', 'p', or 'm' sounds, it becomes 'm'; before 'k' or 'g', it's a 'ng' (as in 'sing'); before vowels or 'y', it's a uvular nasal (made far back in the throat); and before 't', 'd', 'n', it's a regular 'n'. For beginners, just think of it as 'n' — the exact allophone comes naturally with listening practice.
rules: ん counts as one full syllable beat — にほん (Japan) is ni-ho-n, three beats, not two.
ん never starts a word or syllable — it only appears after other syllables.
Its exact sound varies by context (n, m, ng, nasal) but all sound natural with practice.
points.flashcardAnswer: n — a syllabic nasal; one full beat of sound

chapterPractice.prompt: What sound does this character make?
chapterPractice.explanation: ゆ makes the 'yu' sound — a 'y' glide into the flat Japanese 'u'. Remember to keep the vowel flat, not rounded like the English word 'you'. ゆ appears in ゆき (snow) and ゆめ (dream).

chapterPractice.prompt: What does the particle を do in a sentence?
chapterPractice.explanation: を marks the direct object — the noun that receives the action of the verb. For example, ほんをよむ means 'to read a BOOK', where を shows that ほん (book) is the object being read. を is always pronounced 'o' in modern Japanese.

chapterPractice.prompt: Which character makes the 'n' sound AND counts as a full syllable beat on its own?
chapterPractice.explanation: ん is the syllabic nasal — the only hiragana that represents a consonant without a vowel. It counts as a full beat: にほん (Japan) is 3 beats (ni-ho-n), not 2.

わかる (wakaru) means 'to understand' or 'to know'. わ (wa) + か (ka) + る (ru) = wakaru. You'll use this verb constantly — and its negative わかりません (I don't understand) is equally essential. Notice it uses る from the R-row you just learned!
